title: JSON and CSV without surprises
summary: Edit a nested JSON config without flattening it, read the semicolon CSVs Excel writes in half of Europe, and turn text columns into real numbers.

steps.title: JSON in and out
body: ```powershell
$cfg = Get-Content ./appsettings.json -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json     # -Raw: the file as one string
$cfg.Logging.LogLevel.Default                                    # navigate with dots
$cfg.Logging.LogLevel.Default = 'Warning'                         # change a value
$cfg | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 | Set-Content ./appsettings.json  # write it back
`ConvertFrom-Json` turns JSON objects into `PSCustomObject`s and arrays into arrays. With `-AsHashtable` you get
(ordered) hashtables instead, which also allows keys that differ only by case or are empty.
**The trap: `ConvertTo-Json` stops at depth 2 by default.** Anything deeper is replaced by the text of the object,
such as `"@{Enabled=False; Rollout=}"` or `"System.Collections.Hashtable"`. PowerShell 7 prints a warning
(*Resulting JSON is truncated as serialization has exceeded the set depth of 2*); **Windows PowerShell 5.1 truncates
silently.** Always pass `-Depth` (up to 100) when writing anything nested.
Other switches you will use: `-Compress` (one line, for APIs and logs), `-AsArray` (PowerShell 7: an array even
for one object), and `Test-Json` to check text against a JSON schema before you send it.

steps.prompt: A deploy script reads `appsettings.json`, changes one value and writes it back. Afterwards the app fails to start, and the file contains `"NewFlow": "@{Enabled=False; Rollout=}"`. What went wrong?
options: `ConvertTo-Json` ran with its default depth of 2, so deeper objects were written as their text
The file was saved with the wrong encoding
steps.explain: `@{Enabled=False; Rollout=}` is how a PSCustomObject looks as a string: proof that it was turned into text instead of JSON. `ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10` (or more) keeps the structure.

steps.title: Flip a feature flag in appsettings.json
prompt: Release day. In `~/app/appsettings.json`, change exactly these values and nothing else:
Every other setting, including the `Regions` list deep inside, must survive. `jq . ~/app/appsettings.json` shows
the file if you want a second opinion.

checks.name: the log level is Warning
checks.fail: `Logging.LogLevel.Default` should be `"Warning"`, and `Microsoft.AspNetCore` should still be there.

checks.name: the new flow is on at 50%
checks.fail: `Features.Checkout.NewFlow.Enabled` should be `true` and `Rollout.Percent` `50`, as JSON values (not strings).

checks.name: nothing deep was flattened
checks.fail: Some nested settings were lost or turned into text. Look at the file: `"@{...}"` means the JSON was written without enough `-Depth`.

hints: `$cfg = Get-Content ~/app/appsettings.json -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json`, then `$cfg.Features.Checkout.NewFlow` to look around.
Write it back with `$cfg | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 | Set-Content ~/app/appsettings.json`.
steps.explain: Production habit: after writing a config, read it back and validate it before restarting anything: `Get-Content ./appsettings.json -Raw | Test-Json` returns `$true` for valid JSON. And keep the original: `Copy-Item appsettings.json appsettings.json.bak` first costs nothing.
`[pscustomobject]@{...}` keeps the keys in the order written (a plain `@{}` hashtable does not). Numbers and booleans become JSON numbers and booleans; `-Compress` drops the whitespace.

steps.title: CSV: delimiters, culture and types
body: Excel writes CSV with the **list separator of the machine's region**: a comma in the US and UK, a **semicolon** in
Germany, France, the Netherlands and much of Europe, where the comma is the decimal separator (`4,50`).
```powershell
Import-Csv ./stock.csv -Delimiter ';'           # say which separator the file uses
Import-Csv ./stock.csv -UseCulture              # or: the current culture's list separator
Export-Csv ./out.csv -Delimiter ';'             # write one Excel in that region opens correctly
Every field comes back as a **string**. Convert once, right after reading, with a calculated property:
```powershell
$de = [cultureinfo]'de-DE'
Import-Csv ./stock.csv -Delimiter ';' | Select-Object Sku, Name,
@{ n = 'Qty'; e = { [int]$_.Qty } },
@{ n = 'Price'; e = { [decimal]::Parse($_.Price, $de) } }      # '4,50' -> 4.50
Two cousins for other text formats: **`ConvertFrom-StringData`** turns `key=value` lines into a hashtable, and
**`Import-PowerShellDataFile`** safely reads a `.psd1` file (a PowerShell hashtable, the usual format for module
manifests and script settings) without running any code in it.

steps.prompt: Read a German Excel export and keep only items that are low on stock.
steps.explain: Values from `Import-Csv` are strings, and PowerShell converts the right-hand side to the type of the **left-hand** side. So `'9' -lt 10` becomes the text comparison `'9' -lt '10'`, which is `$false`: the item with 9 left would be missed. Cast the left side and it is a number comparison.

hints: `Import-Csv ~/data/stock.csv -Delimiter ';'` reads it. Every field is a string.

`Import-Csv ~/data/stock.csv -Delimiter ';' | Select-Object Sku, Name, @{ n = 'Qty'; e = { [int]$_.Qty } }, @{ n = 'Price'; e = { [decimal]::Parse($_.Price, [cultureinfo]'de-DE') } } | ConvertTo-Json | Set-Content ~/answers/stock.json`
solution: $items = Import-Csv ~/data/stock.csv -Delimiter ';' | Select-Object Sku, Name, @{ n = 'Qty'; e = { [int]$_.Qty } }, @{ n = 'Price'; e = { [decimal]::Parse($_.Price, $de) } }
explain: `ConvertTo-Json -InputObject @($items)` (or `-AsArray`) guarantees an array even if only one row is left on a quiet
day; piping one object would produce a bare object and break the consumer. `[decimal]` is the right type for money:
